title: Short Stuff: The @ Symbol
summary: Short Stuff episode on the @ symbol. The hosts open with banter about obnoxious versus charming trivia, then tour the names for the @ symbol in other languages (Germany, Israel, Hungary, Norway, Turkey, Spain). They explain that the Spanish "arroba" was a unit of measure (about a quarter, roughly 25 pounds, or an amphora-equivalent liquid measure that varied by product and region), traced to Arabic via Moorish influence, and that Greek and Roman amphora trade came before it. They cite Keith Houston's book Shady Characters and an Italian historian, Giorgio Stabile, who found a 1566 letter by Francesco Loppy using the @ sign as shorthand for amphora. In the US the symbol meant "at the rate of" in commerce. It reached typewriters and keyboards late, was added to the BCDIC punch-card code in the 1950s, and was used in IBM's programming code in 1961 on the Stretch supercomputer. Ray Tomlinson picked it for email addresses on ARPANET in 1971, and the episode ends with a promise of a part three and a sign-off.
topics: at the rate of commerce symbol

segments.title: Opening banter and the @ symbol's names
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about obnoxious versus charming trivia, then introduce the @ symbol and its nicknames in other languages, including Germany, Israel, Hungary, Norway and Turkey.

segments.title: Spanish arroba and units of measure
segments.summary: The arroba is a Spanish-speaking market unit of measure whose size varies by product and country. The name is traced to an Arabic word for a quarter, via Moorish influence, and the arroba came to match the amphora.
topics: origin of the at sign name

segments.title: Greek and Roman amphora and Keith Houston's history
segments.summary: Greek and Roman traders used the amphora, a long-necked two-handled jar, as a unit of measure. Keith Houston's book Shady Characters is cited for the history.

segments.title: 1566 letter and the at sign as amphora shorthand
segments.summary: Italian historian Giorgio Stabile found a letter from 1566 by Francesco Loppy in which the @ symbol stood in for amphora. This is the earliest known use, and it shows that arroba and amphora were interchangeable.

segments.title: At the rate of in American commerce and typewriters
segments.summary: In the US the @ symbol became shorthand for 'at the rate of' in commerce. It was not on typewriters until around the turn of the twentieth century, and it was later added to the BCDIC punch-card code in the 1950s.
topics: at the rate of commerce symbol

segments.title: IBM Stretch and Ray Tomlinson's email address
segments.summary: IBM used the @ symbol in its programming code on the Stretch supercomputer in 1961. Ray Tomlinson then used it in ARPANET email addresses in 1971 to separate user from computer, and sent the first test message.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, noting that part three is coming and the show is a production of iHeartRadio and HowStuffWorks.
